title: 4 Things Successful Network Marketing Professionals Do
summary: MLM trainer describes network marketing as word-of-mouth selling, recruiting a team, duplicating and leading, and says anyone coachable can reach the top.

assertions.quote: there is no more powerful form of advertising than a testimonial from somebody that you know

verdicts.note: Referrals convert well, but MLM word of mouth mostly reaches friends and family and exhausts quickly.

In MLM recruiting, personal referrals dominate: 34% of participants were recruited by a friend and 12% by a coworker, versus 6% via a brochure or advertisement; this is about recruitment channels in one industry, not advertising effectiveness generally.

assertions.quote: every time they reorder that distributor gets credit for not only the one order but all future orders

verdicts.note: Plans do pay on reorders, but income disclosures show median distributor commissions near zero because retail customers are few.

A reproduced disclosure lists commissions on sales to Preferred Customers the affiliate sponsors as an income source, so the mechanism exists in at least some MLMs; the same disclosure shows 25% of affiliates received nothing and the lowest rank averaged $504 a year.

Taylor's research finds reselling to non-participants is only a very minor portion of MLM sales because products are priced far above retail alternatives, so recurring customer reorders are rare in practice even if the plan pays on them.

assertions.quote: it'd be better to have a smaller percentage of 100 people than 100 of yourself right

verdicts.note: Income disclosures show downline earnings concentrate in the top one percent and the structure makes most downlines unprofitable.

Downline-based commissions and rank bonuses exist, but the rank tables show over 90% of participants in the lowest cohort averaging under $100 while six-figure incomes belong to hundredths of a percent; the leverage is real only for a tiny fraction.
23% of participants joined specifically to earn by recruiting others, yet only a quarter of all participants ever profited and 47% lost money, so downline income rarely materialises.

Taylor describes the 'leveraged income' pitch and agrees the pay plans route income from a downline, but his data show only about one in 238 participants profit at all and roughly one in 25,000 get the touted residual income.

assertions.quote: you don't get paid for the act of building the team you only get paid when sales happen to a customer

verdicts.note: The report describes MLM pay as commissions for purchasing, inducing others to purchase, or recruiting participants who purchase, with retail resale income only 'in some cases'; it describes the structure but does not measure the split between downline and retail income.

All 30 MLMs with earnings data (and all 350 whose compensation plans Taylor reviewed) pay rewards primarily for recruiting a large downline, not for retailing products, with most payout going to the highest levels.

assertions.quote: you got a whole support system that's not there for a typical entrepreneurial Endeavors

verdicts.note: Uplines do train recruits, but training, events and tools are often sold at a profit and the support is tied to recruiting.

Training exists but is an expense: the FTC lists training materials, conferences and trainings among participant costs, and comments describe paid weekly meetings, $100 conference tickets and required audio subscriptions.
Training seminars and events are counted among the upfront investments participants must pay for, alongside inventory and marketing materials, and participants also spend time attending them.
Training and support exist but Taylor records them as paid 'tools', conferences and meetings sold by upline promoters to recruits, i.e. a cost of participation rather than free support.

assertions.quote: there's nothing that can stop you from going all the way to the top
think about it like setting up franchises all over the world and you're getting a little percentage of all of that stuff

verdicts.note: Unlike franchises, recruits have no territory or customer base and the chain must grow geometrically to pay the levels above.

Taylor cites Commerce Department data that under 4% of franchises fail per year and NFIB data that 39% of small businesses are profitable over their life, against MLM loss rates over 99%; MLMs do not scale like franchises.
